name: Inside a software factory
intro: For engineers who already use Claude Code: what a software factory is, why verification and the three loops matter, and one real request traced through an eleven-stage pipeline on GitLab.
links: Software Factories: The Next Step in AI Coding Isn't the Cloud (Medium)

scenes.kicker: For engineers who already use Claude Code
scenes.title:
Inside a software
factory
scenes.say: What changes when you stop driving every session, and build the machine that does it.
scenes.voice: You already use Claude Code. This is what happens when you stop driving every session yourself, and build a factory that does it: how it's organised, what it checks, and how it gets better.

scenes.title: Three steps
points: An assistant on your laptop. You prompt, you check every edit, the laptop stays on.
A prompt from the app on your phone or desktop, a browser or Slack. One agent, in a cloud sandbox.
Not where the agent runs: how the work is organised, so it can be trusted to run alone.
scenes.voice: AI coding has moved in three steps. First, an assistant on your laptop: you prompt, you check every edit. Then remote agents: you type a prompt in the Claude app on your phone, and it builds in a cloud sandbox. And in parallel, factories: not about where the agent runs, but how the work is organised.

scenes.title: Three ways of working
rows: Usually CI runners (GitLab, GitHub Actions); can run from Claude Code on a laptop
A prompt from the app, a browser or Slack; or an issue assigned to it
An issue in GitLab, GitHub or Jira
You and the AI, in the chat
An agent writes requirements; you approve them first
The agent; some show the plan in the PR
An agent writes a plan, in sections, each with runnable checks
The agent tests its own work; you review the PR

scenes.say: A factory changes who decides, who checks, and what's recorded
scenes.voice: Side by side. Local and remote agents differ mostly in where they run. A factory changes who decides, who checks, and what's recorded: requirements you approve before anything is built, a separate checker agent, evidence for every check, and two approvals instead of one.

scenes.title: Agents write all the code
scenes.define: A software factory is any agentic system where agents write all of the code you ship. Engineers stop building the product, and build the machine that builds it.
scenes.voice: Here's the definition I find most useful, from Dru Knox at Tessl. A software factory is any agentic system where all of the code you ship is written by agents. Your job changes: you stop building the product, and build the machine that builds it.

scenes.title: Autonomy first
points: How often a person has to correct or nudge the agents.
How much can run without anyone reviewing it.
How good the result is for the people who use it.
scenes.voice: How do you measure a factory? Three numbers, in order. Autonomy: how often a person has to correct or nudge the agents. Automation: how much runs without anyone reviewing it. And quality. You earn automation by proving autonomy first.

scenes.title: Verification makes it safe
scenes.define: You can stop reading every line only when something else checks it, every time, and leaves evidence you can inspect. Without that, a factory is a faster way to ship mistakes.
scenes.voice: What makes autonomy safe is verification. You can only stop reading every line if something else checks it, every time, and leaves a record you can inspect. Without that, a factory is just a faster way to ship mistakes.

scenes.title: Three loops
points: Agents iterate before review. Fast and cheap. Raises autonomy.
Thorough checks after the change is up. Replaces review time.
Learns from every correction, and fixes the other two loops.
scenes.voice: And a factory runs in three loops. The inner loop: agents iterate before anything goes up for review, fast and cheap. The outer loop: the thorough checks that replace review time. And the meta loop: it reads the corrections and failures, and fixes the factory itself, so the same mistake doesn't happen twice.

scenes.title: One pipeline, eleven stages
scenes.key: You: two approvalsAgents: requirements, plan, codeScripts: everything checkable
scenes.say: Eleven stages: agents write, scripts check, a person approves twice
scenes.voice: Here's the factory I built, on Claude Code. Eleven stages. Scripts read the issue, lint the plan, re-check the evidence, run the tests, publish a preview, and open the merge request. Agents write the requirements, the plan, and the code. And a person approves twice.

scenes.say: The pipeline is data: who does each stage, and how
scenes.voice: The pipeline is just data. Each stage says who does it, an agent, a script or a human, which skill it follows, and what it may write. A stage can fail three times before the factory stops and asks a person.

scenes.say: A skill: how one kind of job is done
scenes.voice: And each kind of job has a skill: a short written instruction the agent follows. This one is for UI logic. Pure functions, no DOM, no clock. And notice the last line: the maker doesn't tick its own task or write its own evidence.

scenes.title: One request, start to finish
scenes.say: A CRM dashboard, asked for in plain words on a GitLab issue.
scenes.voice: Let's watch one real request go through it.

scenes.say: An issue in plain words, labelled for the factory
scenes.voice: It starts as an issue in GitLab, in plain words, with the factory label. A webhook starts a pass straight away.

scenes.say: The first gate: approve the requirements
scenes.voice: Within a minute the requirements agent has written the request up, and the factory stops at the first gate.

scenes.say: Stories with acceptance criteria every later stage is held to
scenes.voice: Requirements are user stories with acceptance criteria. Everything downstream is checked against these, so this approval actually means something.

scenes.say: Approve: one word on the issue
scenes.voice: The reply is one word on the issue. No slash: GitLab swallows a comment that's only slash-approve.

scenes.say: The plan: sections, skills, and a gate for each
scenes.voice: Then the plan. The work is split into sections, each naming the skill to use, and each ending in a gate the checker must pass.

scenes.where: the checker's checks, written in the plan
scenes.say: Runnable checks, written before the code
scenes.voice: And these are the checker's gates, written in the plan before any code exists. Runnable commands with expected results: the module's exports, no DOM or network access, currency formatting, and totals exact to the cent.

scenes.say: Inner loop: maker builds, a separate checker verifies
scenes.voice: This is the inner loop. A maker session builds a section. A separate checker session, which never saw the maker work, runs the gate. Pass, and the next section starts. Fail, and a fresh maker gets the written findings.

scenes.say: Evidence: what was run, expected, and found
scenes.voice: The checker writes its evidence: each check, expected, found, and a verdict. Four sections in this run, four passes, first time.

scenes.say: Outer loop: evidence re-checked, tests, preview
scenes.voice: Then the outer loop: a script re-runs the evidence checks rather than trusting them, the full test suite runs, and a preview goes up.

scenes.say: Try it: the real change, running
scenes.voice: The person who asked tries the real thing in a browser, and approves again.

scenes.say: A merge request with the specs and evidence
scenes.voice: And a merge request opens, with the specs and every evidence file linked. Merging stays with a human.

scenes.title: Issue in, merge request out
scenes.key: Nothing on your laptop. Each pass is stateless; its state lives in git.
scenes.say: Webhook, runner, flow.py, claude -p, state in git
scenes.voice: How it runs. A GitLab issue or comment fires a webhook. That starts a pipeline on a runner. Each pass restores the factory's state from a branch, runs flow dot py through the stages, launches claude dash p for each agent stage, pushes the work branch, comments on the issue, and saves its state again.

scenes.title: The loops, made concrete
points: Maker and checker per section; a failed gate goes back with findings, up to three tries.
Evidence re-checked by script, presubmit, preview, then a person tries it.
Every intervention is recorded; fixes go into skills and rules. By hand, for now.
scenes.voice: Mapped to the loops. Inner loop: maker and checker per section, three attempts. Outer loop: scripts and tests, then a person tries it. And the meta loop: every time a person has to step in, it's recorded on the issue, and the fix goes into a skill or the rules. Honestly, today that loop is me, by hand.

scenes.title: Issue to merge request
numbers: issue to merge request, approvals included
sections passed their checker first time
scenes.say: 17 minutes, 10 agent sessions, about $1.24, 4 of 4 first time
scenes.voice: The numbers from that run. Seventeen minutes from issue to merge request, approvals included. Ten agent runs. About a dollar twenty at API prices. And every section passed its checker first time.

scenes.title: What it doesn't do yet
points: Checks prove the checks pass, not that the spec was right.
Still run by hand: interventions are recorded, fixes are manual.
One request at a time on the runner.
scenes.voice: And the limits. Checks prove the checks pass, not that the spec was right, which is why a person approves it. The meta loop is still manual. The runner works one request at a time. And it's best on small, clear requests.

scenes.title: Get a playground
scenes.say: Your own GitLab project, nothing to install. The code: github.com/sanjeev23oct/software-factory
scenes.voice: Want to try it? There's a playground: your own GitLab project, nothing to install. File an issue and watch it go through. The code is open source, and the longer read is on Medium.
